'''''Cymbalaria muralis''''', commonly called '''ivy-leaved toadflax''',<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020>{{cite web |title=Ivy-leaved Toadflax ''Cymbalaria muralis'' |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor1=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |date=2020 |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.vcr |access-date=17 March 2024 }}</ref> is a low, spreading, trailing plant with small purple flowers, native to rocky habitats in southern Europe. It belongs to the plantain family ([[Plantaginaceae]]), and is introduced and [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in many other temperate locations. The flower stalk is unusual for seeking light until it is fertilized, after which it grows away from the light. Other names include '''coliseum ivy''', '''Kenilworth ivy''', '''mother of thousands''', '''Oxford ivy''', and '''wandering sailor'''.

==Description==
''Cymbalaria muralis'' spreads quickly, growing {{convert|10–80|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="Flora British" /><ref name="FNA">{{cite web |last1=Elisens |first1=Wayne J. |title=''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''muralis'' - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Cymbalaria_muralis_subsp._muralis |website=Flora of North America |access-date=3 January 2024 |date=5 November 2020}}</ref><ref name="PerennialGC">{{cite book |last1=MacKenzie |first1=David S. |title=Perennial ground covers |date=1997 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |isbn=978-0-88192-368-1 |pages=121–122 |edition=1st |url=https://archive.org/details/perennialgroundc0000mack/page/121 |access-date=3 January 2024}}</ref> It is a [[biennial plant|biennial]] or short lived [[perennial plant]].<ref name="Peirce" /> Its roots are thin and fibrous for reaching into cracks.<ref name="New British" /> Its rounded, heart-shaped, or kidney shaped leaves are 5–40 mm long, 6–60 mm wide, and are alternating, supported on thin [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s, usually purple, 10–22 mm long.<ref name="Flora British" /><ref name="PerennialGC" /><ref name="FNA" /> The leaves are either smooth (glabrous) or with widely scattered hairs in the subspecies ''muralis'',<ref name="FNA" /> or pubescent ([[villous]]) in the subspecies ''visianii''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Polunin |first1=Oleg |title=Flowers of Greece and the Balkans : A Field Guide |date=1980 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford; New York |isbn=978-0-19-217626-4 |page=189 |url=https://archive.org/details/flowersofgreeceb0000polu/page/189 |access-date=3 January 2024}}</ref> They may have from three to seven lobes,<ref name="PerennialGC" /> but most often has five lobes.<ref name="Flora British" /> The leaves are relatively thick and often blushed with purple on their undersides.<ref name="Flora British" />

''Cymbalaria muralis'' has small flowers that strongly resemble those of a [[snapdragon]].<ref name="PerennialGC" /> They have [[sepal]]s at the base of the flower that have lobes 1.5–3 mm long and are sharply pointed. The [[petal]]s form a closed tube 3–5 mm long. The lower lip of the flower expanded upwards to block the tube of the flower similarly to the well known snapdragon flowers (palate inflated). The two cushion shaped parts of the lip under the mouth have yellow spots.<ref name="Flora British" /> The lower lobes of the flower are spreading while the upper ones stand up, with rounded ends and 2–3 mm long.<ref name="FNA" /> The majority of the flower is lilac with a yellow throat<ref name="PerennialGC" /> with darker lines on the upper lobes.<ref name="Flora British" /> Rarely the flowers may be all or nearly all white. At the rear of the flower there is a short [[Spur (botany)|spur]] about a third of the total length of the flower.<ref name="Flora British" />

Flowering is dependent on local conditions. In Britain it may flower from May until the end of November,<ref name="Plant Associations">{{cite book |last1=Maidment |first1=Clem |title=Plant Associations : An Introduction to British Wild Plants and Their Environmental and Human Associations |date=2007 |publisher=Greenditch Press |location=Radstock, United Kingdom |isbn=978-0-9554947-0-3 |page=57 |edition=1st |url=https://archive.org/details/plantassociation0000maid/page/57 |access-date=9 January 2024}}</ref> while in Eastern Europe it does so from June to July with seeds in September.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kuprianova |first1=L.A. |editor1-last=Komaroav |editor1-first=V.L |editor2-last=Schischkin |editor2-first=B.K. |editor3-last=Bobrov |editor3-first=E.G. |editor4-last=Shetler |editor4-first=Stanwyn G. |editor5-last=Fet |editor5-first=Galina N. |title=Flora of the U.S.S.R |date=1968 |publisher=Israel Program for Scientific Translations |location=Jerusalem, Israel |page=156 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/floraofussr22bota/page/156 |access-date=9 January 2024 |language=en |volume=XXII : Solanaceae and Scrophulariacea |chapter=Genus 1326. CYMBALARIA Medic}}</ref> In North America it may flower from May to October.<ref name="FNA" /> In New Zealand it flowers all year long, from January to December.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Breitwieser |first1=I. |last2=Heenan |first2=P.J. |last3=Nelson |first3=W.A. |last4=Wilton |first4=A.D. |title=Taxon Profile Cymbalaria muralis (based on Heenan 2014) |url=https://www.nzflora.info/factsheet/Taxon/Cymbalaria-muralis.html |website=Flora of New Zealand Online |access-date=6 January 2024 |language=en |date=2010–2024}}</ref>

The flowers are pollinated by bees, but are also self-compatible.<ref name="Flora British" /> Once a flower is fertilized it forms a globular capsule 3–5 mm in diameter.<ref name="FNA" /> Each of the capsules has two openings, each with three valves.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=Arthur Roy |last2=Tutin |first2=Thomas Gaskell |last3=Warburg |first3=Edmund Frederic |author1-link=Arthur Roy Clapham |author2-link=Thomas Gaskell Tutin |author3-link=E. F. Warburg |title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles |date=1968 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, United Kingdom; London |isbn=978-0-521-04656-5 |page=320 |edition=2nd |url=https://archive.org/details/excursionfloraof0000clap/page/320 |access-date=6 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref> The seeds are quite small, just 0.5–1 mm with a crescent shape covered in minute warty bumps.<ref name="FNA" /> This plant has an unusual method for planting its own seeds. The flower stalk is initially positively [[phototropic]] and moves towards the light. After fertilisation, it becomes negatively phototropic ("scototropic") and moves away from the light. This results in seed capsules being pushed into dark crevices of rock walls, where it is more likely to germinate.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hart |first1=James Watnell |title=Plant Tropisms and Other Growth Movements |date=1992 |publisher=Chapman & Hall |location=London; New York |isbn=978-0-412-53080-7 |page=101 |edition=Reprint |url=https://archive.org/details/planttropismsoth0000hart_q2s1/page/101 |access-date=6 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Cymbalaria muralis Sturm21.jpg|thumb|right|''Cymbalaria muralis'' botanical illustration from ''Deutschlands Flora in Abbildungen'', 1796]]
As with many plants, ''Cymbalaria muralis'' was given its first scientific name and description by the early taxonomist [[Carl Linnaeus]]. He placed it in the genus ''[[Antirrhinum]]'' with plants commonly called snapdragons in 1753 as ''Antirrhinum cymbalaria''. Its taxonomic history since that date is quite complex with twenty-two species and five subspecies that are considered to be [[taxonomic synonym]]s as of 2024.<ref name="POWO" />

The very first is a reclassification in genus ''[[Linaria]]'', the toadflaxes, as ''Linaria cymbalaria'' by the botanist [[Philip Miller]] in 1768. Four other names were published after this in ''Linaria'' that had acceptance for a time and ''Linaria cymbalaria'' continued to be used alongside other names as late as 1902.<ref name="POWO" />

A spelling variation (see [[Orthographical variant]]) created by the botanist [[Noël Martin Joseph de Necker]] 1773 when he spelled it ''Antirrhinum cimbalaria''. The species was described and given a taxonomic [[superfluous name]] six years later in 1779 by the naturalist [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] as ''Antirrhinum hederaceum''. Likewise the botanist [[Richard Anthony Salisbury]] gave it a similar superfluous name, ''Antirrhinum hederifolium'', in 1796. It was described four more times under different names in ''Antirrhinum'' in the 1800s.<ref name="POWO" />

It was described by [[Philipp Gottfried Gaertner]], [[Bernhard Meyer]], and [[Johannes Scherbius]] with a new classification as ''Cymbalaria muralis'' in 1800.<ref name="POWO" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Gärtner |first1=Gottfried |last2=Meyer |first2=Bernhard |last3=Scherbius |first3=Johannes |author1-link=Philipp Gottfried Gaertner |author2-link=Bernhard Meyer |author3-link=Johannes Scherbius |title=Oekonomisch-technische Flora der Wetterau |date=1799 |publisher=P. H. Guilhauman |location=Frankfurt am Main |pages=397–398 |url=https://archive.org/details/oekonomischtechn02gr/page/397 |access-date=3 January 2024 |language=de |volume=2}}</ref> As previously it was given six more variously incorrect names in genus ''[[Cymbalaria]]'' over the next 147 years.<ref name="POWO" />

As of 2024 [[Plants of the World Online]] (POWO), [[World Flora Online]] (WFO), and the [[Flora of North America]], all list ''Cymbalaria muralis'' as the correct name for this species.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="WFO" /><ref name="FNA" />

===Subspecies===
As of 2024 there are two widely accepted subspecies. The [[Autonym (botany)|autonym]] ''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''muralis'' and ''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''visianii''.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="WFO">{{Cite WFO |title=''Cymbalaria muralis'' G.Gaertn., B.Mey. & Scherb. |id=0000632510 |access-date=1 January 2024}}</ref> In some sources ''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''pubescens'' continues to be listed as a valid subspecies, but it is not listed as valid by most sources.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Marhold |first1=Karol |title=''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''pubescens'' |url=https://europlusmed.org/cdm_dataportal/taxon/f9c9a5d6-3d22-4333-9409-399523066590 |website=Euro+Med-Plantbase |access-date=9 January 2024}}</ref>

====''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''muralis''====
This subspecies is hairless or nearly so in most parts.<ref name="FNA" /> It is widespread and commonly encountered across much of the temperate world, see distribution for details.<ref name="POWO ssp muralis">{{cite POWO |id=77229381-1 |title=''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''muralis'' |access-date=5 January 2024}}</ref>

====''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''visianii''====
This subspecies was first described in 1925 as ''Cymbalaria muralis'' f. ''visianii'' by [[Sándor Jávorka]] using an incomplete description by Jenő Béla Kümmerle.<ref name="POWO ssp visianii">{{cite POWO |id=891253-1 |title=''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''visianii'' (Kümmerle ex Jáv.) D.A.Webb |access-date=5 January 2024}}</ref> In 1972 the Irish botanist [[D. A. Webb]] described it with its current name making the distinction from ''Cymbalaria pilosa'', which as of 2024 is regarded as a synonym of ''[[Sibthorpia europaea]]'' by POWO.<ref>{{cite POWO |id=809676-1 |title=''Sibthorpia europaea'' L. |access-date=4 January 2024}}</ref> All parts of the plants are covered in fine hairs (villous) except for the seed pods, which are hairless.<ref name="Linnean Soc.">{{cite journal |last1=Heywood |first1=V. H. |title=Flora Europaea: Notulae Systematicae ad Floram Europaeam spectantes: No. 12 |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |date=April 1972 |volume=65 |issue=2 |page=265 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.1972.tb00935.x}}</ref>

===Names===
[[File:Cymbalaria February 2008-1.jpg|thumb|right|''Cymbalaria muralis'' flower side view]]
The species name ''muralis'' comes from the Latin "mūrālis" for walls and relating to them, from its habit of growing on them.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lewis |first1=Charlton T. |last2=Short |first2=Charles |title=A Latin Dictionary |date=1879 |publisher=Clarendon Press |location=Oxford, United Kingdom |page=1177 |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.61236/page/n1196 |access-date=4 January 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Harrison |first1=Lorraine |title=Latin for Gardeners : Over 3000 Plant Names Explained and Explored |date=2012 |publisher=The University of Chicago Press |location=Chicago, Illinois |isbn=978-0-226-00919-3 |pages=42, 139 |url=https://archive.org/details/latinforgardener0000harr/page/139 |access-date=4 January 2024}}</ref>

One of its most frequent common names in English, "ivy-leaved toadflax", is a compound name that describes the appearance of the plant. The leaves of the species are similar shape to those of [[Hedera|ivy]]. Its flowers are similar to those of the closely related genus ''[[Linaria]]'', which is called toadflax because it is a frequent weed of [[flax]] grown as a crop, and the flowers reminded people of a toad's mouth.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Painter |first1=Gilian |title=A Garden of Old Fashioned and Unusual Herbs |date=1982 |publisher=Hodder and Stoughton |location=Auckland, New Zealand; London; Sydney, Australia |isbn=978-0-340-27224-4 |pages=221–223 |edition=1st |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenofoldfashi0000pain/page/221 |access-date=5 January 2024}}</ref>

Related to its habit of growing on ruins, it was also called "coliseum ivy", a name that was first recorded in 1864.<ref name="Peirce" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Rand Jr. |first1=Edward Sprague |title=Flowers for the Parlor and Garden |date=1864 |publisher=J. E. Tilton & Co. |location=Boston, Massachusetts |page=254 |url=https://archive.org/details/flowersforparlo01randgoog/page/n262 |access-date=4 January 2024}}</ref> From its first location of introduction in England it was also called "Oxford ivy" and was previously called "Oxford weed".<ref name="Plant-Book">{{cite book |last1=Mabberley |first1=D. J. |author1-link=David Mabberley |title=The Plant-Book : A Portable Dictionary of the Vascular Plants |date=1998 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, United Kingdom; New York |isbn=978-0-521-41421-0 |page=205 |edition=2nd |url=https://archive.org/details/plantbookportabl0000mabb_w8f6/page/205 |access-date=5 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref> The common name "Kenilworth ivy" is speculated to come from the English town of [[Kenilworth]] or the castle of the same name which is near where the plant first appeared in England in the 1600s.<ref name="Peirce">{{cite book |last1=Peirce |first1=Pam |title=Wildly Successful Plants : Northern California Gardens |date=2004 |publisher=Sasquatch Books |location=Seattle, Washington |isbn=978-1-57061-358-6 |pages=130–134 |edition=1st |url=https://archive.org/details/wildlysuccessful0000peir/page/130 |access-date=3 January 2024}}</ref> Other less common names related to its ivy-like appearance include "ivy-weed", "ivy-wort", and "Kentucky-ivy".<ref name="Common Names">{{cite book |last1=Carleton |first1=R. Milton |title=Index to the Common Names of Herbaceous Plants |date=1962 |publisher=The Shoe String Press |location=Hamden, Connecticut |pages=23, 28, 29, 37, 45, 67, 69, 83, 89, 91, 100, 121 |edition=Reprint |url=https://archive.org/details/indextocommonnam0000unse_j5m6 |access-date=5 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref> The common name "mother of thousands" has been applied to this species and also to ''[[Saxifraga stolonifera]]'', ''[[Tolmiea menziesii]]'', and ''[[Soleirolia soleirolii]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Whitmore |first1=Patrick |title=The Common Names of Wild Flowers in English and French |date=1991 |publisher=Packard Publishing Limited |location=Chichester, United Kingdom |isbn=978-1-85341-027-7 |page=19 |edition=1st |url=https://archive.org/details/commonnamesofwil0000whit/page/19 |access-date=3 January 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Conder |first1=Susan |title=Terence Conran's Decorating With Plants |date=1990 |publisher=Gallery Books : Pub. by W.H. Smith |location=New York |isbn=978-0-8317-2169-5 |url=https://archive.org/details/terenceconransde0000cond/page/34 |access-date=3 January 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Thompson |first1=Ken |title=The Book of Weeds |date=2009 |publisher=DK |location=London; New York |isbn=978-0-7566-4271-6 |page=114 |url=https://archive.org/details/bookofweeds0000thom_g0h7/page/114 |access-date=3 January 2024}}</ref> It has also been called "pennywort", but this name is shared with many other vaguely round leafed herbaceous plants.<ref name="Plant-Book" /><ref name="Common Names" /> Less common names shared with other plants include "cancer root" (with ''[[Conopholis americana]]'' and ''[[Epifagus virginiana]]''),<ref name="Common Names" /> and "wandering sailor"<ref name="Plant-Book" /> (with genus ''[[Lysimachia]]''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Le Strange |first1=Richard |title=A History of Herbal Plants |date=1977 |publisher=Arco Publishing Company |location=New York |isbn=978-0-668-04247-5 |page=170 |url=https://archive.org/details/historyofherbalp0000lest_x7u7/page/170 |access-date=5 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref>), and "Wandering Jew" (with ''[[Saxifraga stolonifera]]'' and ''[[Tradescantia fluminensis]]'').<ref name="Common Names" /> Two other nautical names include "climbing sailor" and "roving sailor".<ref name="Common Names" /> It has also been called "pedlar's basket", "rabbits", "roving Jenny", and "Devil's ribbon".<ref name="New British">{{cite book |last1=Horwood |first1=Arthur Reginald |last2=Fitch |first2=John Nugent |title=A New British Flora; British Wild Flowers in Their Natural Haunts |date=1919 |publisher=Gresham Publishing Company, Ltd. |location=London |pages=170–171 |url=https://archive.org/details/newbritishflorab05horw/page/170 |access-date=6 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Common Names" />

==Distribution==
[[File:Muurleeuwenbek (Cymbalaria muralis).jpg|thumb|right|''Cymbalaria muralis'' growing on a wall]]
POWO regards the native range for this species to be limited to southern Europe, in Austria, France, Italy, Switzerland, and the former Yugoslavia, with the nominate subspecies ''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''muralis'' also occurring throughout this range.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="POWO ssp muralis" /> Similarly the World Plants database records it as native to the same areas, but more specifically to Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia & Hercegovina, Serbia, and Kosovo in the former Yugoslavia and to the small state of San Marino on the Italian peninsula. It also shows it as native to additional areas north east of the Alps such as the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Liechtenstein, and many Atlantic Ocean islands such as the [[Azores]], [[Madeira]], the [[Canary Islands]], and the [[Cape Verde Islands]].<ref name="WorldPlants">{{cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=Michael |title=''Cymbalaria'' |url=https://www.worldplants.de/world-plants-complete-list/complete-plant-list#plantUid-316621 |website=World Plants. Synonymic Checklist and Distribution of the World Flora. Version 18.3 |access-date=5 January 2024 |date=3 January 2024}}</ref>

''Cymbalaria muralis'' subsp. ''visianii'' recorded by POWO as growing in the southeastern part of the species' range, only in Italy and the former Yugoslavia.<ref name="POWO ssp visianii" /> The World Plants database largely agrees listing it as native to the central and southern parts of Italy and to Croatia, but also listing it as introduced in Germany;<ref name="WorldPlants" /> it has also been recorded as naturalised in Britain since 1970.<ref name=BSBI_Atlas2020 />

[[File:Cymbalaria muralis kz05.jpg|thumb|left|''Cymbalaria muralis'' seedling in the [[Berlin Botanical Gardens]]]]
From this original range it spread to much of Europe and to the rest of the world as either an accidental introduction or because of its use as an ornamental plant.<ref name="Poland">{{cite book |last1=Szczęśniak |first1=Ewa |last2=Świerkosz |first2=Krzysztof |editor1-last=Zając |editor1-first=Adam |editor2-last=Zając |editor2-first=Maria |editor3-last=Zemanek |editor3-first=Bogdan |title=Phytogeographical Problems of Synanthropic Plants |date=2003 |publisher=Jagiellonian University |location=Cracow, Poland |doi=10.6084/M9.FIGSHARE.105653 |isbn=8391516148 |pages=185–193 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/309240842 |access-date=5 January 2024 |language=en |chapter=''Cymbalaria muralis'' P. Gaertn., B. Mey. & Schreb. and ''Cymbalarietum muralis'' Görs 1966 in Lower Silesia – expansion or regression?}}</ref> Its first record outside of cultivation in Great Britain is from 1640.<ref name="Flora British">{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=A. R. (Arthur Roy) |title=Flora of the British Isles |date=1987 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge, UK; New York, NY |isbn=978-0-521-30985-1 |pages=373–374 |url=https://archive.org/details/floraofbritishis0000clap/page/373 |access-date=4 January 2024}}</ref> A frequently repeated story is that the plants were introduced accidentally as part of a shipment of statuary to Oxford.<ref name="Plant-Book" /> However, this is unlikely since it was recorded growing in an English garden in 1617 in [[Droxford]].<ref name="Scotland">{{cite journal |last1=Watt |first1=Hugh Boyd |title=Notes on the Introduction and Distribution of ''Cymbalaria muralis'' G.Gaertn., B.Mey. & Scherb. in Scotland |journal=Proceedings of the Botanical Society of the British Isles |date=1956 |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=123–125 |url=https://archive.org/details/proceedingsofbot02bota_0/page/123 |access-date=6 January 2024 |publisher=London}}</ref> Thereafter it became a popular ornamental plant that was widely planted in the United Kingdom through the 19th century.<ref name="FloraBritannica">{{cite book |last1=Mabey |first1=Richard |title=Flora Britannica |date=1996 |publisher=Sinclair-Stevenson |location=London |isbn=978-1-85619-377-1 |page=331 |edition=1. publ}}</ref> Regardless of its status it is recorded from Ireland and Portugal in the west in every country as far east as Ukraine, Poland, and Sweden, and according to POWO it may also be found in the Baltic States, northwestern Russia, and the North Caucasus<ref name="POWO" /> with World Plants recording it in Belarus and Georgia.<ref name="WorldPlants" />

In Africa it grows in Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia in the north and in South Africa it grows in the [[Cape Provinces]] and the [[Northern Provinces]] floristic areas. In Asia it is now found in Turkey, Jordan, North Korea, South Korea, and the eastern Himalayas.<ref name="POWO" />

In North America ''Cymbalaria muralis'' has been recorded growing outside cultivation in Bermuda, Canada, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, and the United States.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="WorldPlants" /> In the USA it is generally agreed that it grows in much of the [[Midwest]], north-east, and New England as far south as South Carolina, Tennessee, and Arkansas and as far west as Wisconsin, Illinois, and Missouri with the exception of Maine and New Hampshire. It is also found on the west coast in California, Oregon, and Washington State. It is more scattered in the interior states, listed as growing in Colorado, Nebraska, South Dakota, and Utah, with the last of these recorded by USDA [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]] PLANTS database (PLANTS) and World Plants, but not POWO.<ref name="USDA">{{cite usda plants|symbol=CYMU |title=''Cymbalaria muralis'' |date=6 January 2024}}</ref><ref name="POWO" /><ref name="WorldPlants" /> In Canada it agreed that it grows in five provinces, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Ontario, and Québec. However PLANTS and World Plants also record it in Nova Scotia<ref name="USDA" /><ref name="WorldPlants" /> while POWO alone records it on the island of Newfoundland.<ref name="POWO" />

In South America it has been observed in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru in the north.<ref name="WorldPlants" /> It has also been recorded in the south and southeast of Brazil, Uruguay, Bolivia, and the north of Argentina.<ref name="POWO" /> In mainland Chile it has been reported from [[Valparaíso]], in [[Santiago]], the [[Maule Region]], and the [[Biobío Region]].<ref name="WorldPlants" />

On oceanic islands it has been introduced to Maui in Hawaii,<ref name="USDA" /><ref name="WorldPlants" /> both the North and South Island of New Zealand,<ref name="AVH">{{cite web |last1=AVH |title=''Cymbalaria muralis'' |url=https://avh.ala.org.au/occurrences/search?taxa=Cymbalaria+muralis#tab_mapView |website=The Australasian Virtual Herbarium |publisher=Council of Heads of Australasian Herbaria |access-date=6 January 2024 |language=en |date=2024}}</ref> Bermuda, Mauritius, St. Helena,<ref name="POWO" /> and the Juan Fernández Islands.<ref name="WorldPlants" /> It is also found in six Australian states, Western Australia, South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales, the south of Queensland, and the island state of Tasmania.<ref name="AVH" />

==Habitat==
[[Image:Cymbalaria muralis G.Gaertn., B.Mey. and Schreb. (AM AK297660-1).jpg|thumb|[[Epiphyte|Epiphytic]] upon the trunk of a [[Arecaceae|palm tree]], [[Auckland]], NZ]]
The original habitat for ''Cymbalaria muralis'' was narrow niches in rock faces and cliffs.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rieley |first1=Jack |last2=Page |first2=Susan |title=Ecology of Plant Communities : A Phytosociological Account of British Vegetation |date=1990 |publisher=Longman Scientific & Technical |location=Harlow, Essex, United Kingdom |page=154 |url=https://archive.org/details/ecologyofplantco0000riel/page/154 |access-date=6 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref>
In cooler climates like [[Lower Silesia]] in Poland it grows in warm [[microclimate]]s such as on south or west facing walls of structures or the embankments of rivers.<ref name="Poland" /> It is considered very characteristic of the vegetation that grows on walls.<ref name="Wall Vegetation">{{cite book |last1=Segal |first1=S. |title=Notes on Wall Vegetation |date=1969 |publisher=D. W. Junk N.V. |location=Hague, Netherlands |pages=12, 51, 52 |url=https://archive.org/details/notesonwallveget0000sseg/page/12 |access-date=9 January 2024}}</ref>

In hot climates it becomes a high altitude specialist, for example growing from 1100–1300 m in elevation in Costa Rica.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barringer |first1=Kerry |last2=Burger |first2=William C. |title=Flora Costaricensis: Family #193. Scrophulariaceae |journal=Fieldiana Botany |date=2000 |volume=41 |page=36 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/20419#page/42 |access-date=6 January 2024 |publisher=Field Museum of Natural History |location=Chicago, Illinois}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Cymbalaria muralis'' is a generalist, attracting a wide range of pollinators, including bees, flies, and butterflies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guzmán |first1=B. |last2=Gómez |first2=J. M. |last3=Vargas |first3=P. |title=Is floral morphology a good predictor of floral visitors to Antirrhineae (snapdragons and relatives)? |journal=Plant Biology |date=July 2017 |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=515–524 |doi=10.1111/plb.12567|pmid=28316136 |bibcode=2017PlBio..19..515G }}</ref> Their roots are associated with [[arbuscular mycorrhiza]], a group of fungi that partner with plants.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Harley |first1=J. L. |last2=Harley |first2=E. L. |title=A Check-list of Mycorrhiza in the British Flora |journal=New Phytologist |date=February 1987 |volume=105 |issue=s1 |page=69 |doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.1987.tb00674.x}}</ref>

At least three aphid species ''[[Myzus ornatus]]'' (violet aphid), ''[[Myzus persicae]]'' (green peach aphid), and ''[[Myzus cymbalariae]]'' are commonly found on ''Cymbalaria muralis''. The last of these was first observed feeding on ivy-leaved toadflax and is named for the species.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stroyan |first1=H. L. G. |title=A Replacement Name in ''Myzus'' Passerini (Homoptera: Aphidoidea) |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Entomological Society of London. Series B, Taxonomy |date=December 1967 |volume=36 |issue=11–12 |pages=186 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-3113.1967.tb00536.x}}</ref> The plant is also a host for tomato ringspot virus.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hildebrand |first1=E.M. |title=Tomato Ringspot on Currant |journal=American Journal of Botany |date=1942 |volume=29 |issue=5 |page=363 |doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1942.tb14230.x |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.270745/page/n372 |access-date=11 January 2024}}</ref>

==Uses==
===Edibility===
Ivy-leaved toadflax is sometimes used as a salad green in Southern Europe.<ref name="Plant Associations" /> Its taste is described as like raw garden peas<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pond |first1=Barbara |title=A Sampler of Wayside Herbs : Rediscovering Old Uses for Familiar Wild Plants |date=1982 |publisher=Greenwich House |location=New York |isbn=978-0-517-38594-4 |page=84 |url=https://archive.org/details/samplerofwayside00pond/page/84 |access-date=9 January 2024}}</ref> or bitter with a sharp numbing sensation,<ref name="Plant Associations" /> however it has also been noted as slightly toxic by researchers Marion Cooper and Anthony Johnson.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Cymbalaria muralis'' Kenilworth Ivy |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Cymbalaria+muralis |website=PFAF Plant Database |access-date=9 January 2024}}</ref>

===Cultivation===
In gardens ivy-leaved toadflax is planted as a [[groundcover]], particularly on rocky slopes, and planted in wall cracks. Once established it will reproduce on its own, both from seeding and stems rooting themselves.<ref name="Peirce" />  It is winter hardy in [[USDA zone]]s 5 to 9.<ref name="PerennialGC" /> According to the garden author Carolyn Singer it is deer resistant.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Singer |first1=Carolyn |title=Deer in My Garden : Volume 2: Groundcovers & Edgers |date=2009 |publisher=Garden Wisdom Press |isbn=978-0-9774251-5-0 |pages=85–87 |url=https://archive.org/details/deerinmygardenvo0000unse/page/84 |access-date=3 January 2024}}</ref>
